meta.subtitle: Season four in four tiers, from the guy who trusts the points.

threads.note: The column ranked Zach first and picked him to win the title in writing. By the league's own jinx theology, a public blessing from Blake is an attack. The season grades both the pick and the spell.
threads.title: The Blessing

threads.note: Three champions in three seasons and nobody twice. Ben is the third man to carry a title into a new year, ranked sixth by his own leaguemate. The column's call is that he does not repeat.
threads.title: The Repeat

threads.note: Kevin established in February that Sleeper counts a two-way player's receiving production in the DB slot. Nate spent the 1.04 on it. Ben raised deleting the slot outright. The NFL's owners kept the tush push by two votes in May; this league's version is still unscheduled.
threads.title: The DB Slot

threads.note: Zach and Harlow agreed a starting DB is worth about ten points a week. Harlow then set Hunter's bar at 15+. Kevin's independent break-even, four catches for sixty yards and 0.4 touchdowns, comes to 10.4 and matches the agreed baseline. The season settles which number was right.
threads.title: Ten Points, Not Fifteen

threads.note: Brent has run this league since it started and never won it. Over the fourteen weeks that decided the 2024 standings he outscored every team except Zach and finished 7-9. The column ranked him third on the roster Patrick called the league's oldest back in 2023.
threads.title: The Commissioner's Ring

threads.note: The column ranked Kevin fifth off a 5-12 season and put the playoff call on the record. His records have run under his rosters for three straight years.
threads.title: Noble Makes the Playoffs

threads.note: David rosters five quarterbacks in a league that starts one and does not answer trade texts. The column's call: he does not trade a single one before the deadline, and it costs him a playoff spot.
threads.title: Father Time Collects Quarterbacks

threads.note: Harlow holds Nate's 2026 first and second, the league's only genuine short position on the guarantee. The column ranked him twelfth and called its own ranking wrong, on the record: Harlow finishes ahead of David.
threads.title: The Short Position

threads.note: Three years of accumulated capital became eleven picks and the first overall. The column's calls: Chudders is not last, and wins more games than in any season in franchise history.
threads.title: Chudders Cashes In

threads.note: The columnist's four-quarterback room already lost one job before kickoff. His own call, against himself: at least two of the four are not starting NFL games by Thanksgiving.
threads.title: The Quarterback Tax

threads.note: Nate called the Anthony Richardson pick bad in September 2023 and said it would stay true all year. Indianapolis handed the job to Daniel Jones on August 19. Settled, and conceded in print.
threads.title: The Richardson Receipt

threads.note: The November 2023 tank has never been ruled on because there is no rule. In December 2024 Nate told the room about the all-natural first-year tank job in his Ohio league. The precedent is alive and the man is proud of the craft.
threads.title: No Rule Against It

meta.title: Preseason 2025

rankings.blurb:
Tier one is two teams and I own the other one, so let me get the conflict of interest out of the way: I ran the numbers every way I know how this summer and they cannot separate Zach and me, and I am religiously barred from picking myself. So Zach is first, and I mean it, and he is going to hate that I mean it.

Here is what the standings never told you. Over the fourteen weeks that decided the 2024 season, Zach outscored all of us. Not most of us. All of us. Then he lost the final by 5.70 points on a Monday night when his title chances came down to Kaden Ellis against George Kittle, and he handled it better than any of us would have. "I doomed myself when I pulled Brian burns for deforest Buckner. I put my giant to sleep. You deserve this Ben". The same night, before the trophy was even engraved, he posted "I’ve got 4 top 15 RBs and need picks and youth at WR. Open to trades. Let the offseason begin!" The man grieves in trade ads.

Then he ran the whole thing back, and the league he plays in cooperated. Baltimore handed Derrick Henry a two-year extension in May, the biggest ever given a back past thirty, after Henry put up 1,921 yards at age thirty. The Rams extended Kyren Williams in August off back-to-back 1,100-yard seasons. Josh Jacobs opened Packers camp announcing "I'm sick" about not having a trophy. Jalen Hurts is coming off a Super Bowl. Mike Evans needs one more thousand-yard season to pass Jerry Rice, and Rice personally blessed the attempt. Zach's answer, "Henrys gonna go til he’s 40 tho", reads like a joke and doubles as the franchise thesis, and every NFL front office that touched his roster this offseason co-signed it.

The warts are real. Cooper Kupp is in Seattle now catching balls from Sam Darnold, which is also Zach's stack, on purpose, because he cannot help himself. Jordan Addison opens the year suspended three games. The whole build is old enough that a fire sale tomorrow would fetch almost nothing, which is a problem for 2027 and irrelevant to the only question this column ranks on.

So here is the call, and Zach will recognize it for exactly what it is. Sleeping Giants wins the 2025 title. In writing. On the record. You were destined, buddy.

Writing this capsule is a trap and everyone reading it knows why. Zach put my tell, the reverse jinx, on the record back in 2023, so if I talk this roster up I am bragging on my own site, and if I talk it down the room files it as spellwork. There is no version of this paragraph I win. So I will just do the audit.

The case for: I won the 2023 title, only Zach and Brent outscored me across the fourteen weeks that decided last season, and the wideout room runs six deep. CeeDee Lamb just got handed George Pickens as a running mate, which Dallas paid Pittsburgh real draft capital for in May. Saquon Barkley signed the first twenty-million-a-year running back contract in history off a 2,005-yard season. That is the floor.

The case against has kept its job for three seasons: the quarterbacks. There are four of them, and the season already benched one. Indianapolis gave Daniel Jones the job on August 19, which closes a receipt Nate opened in September 2023 when he wrote "Richardson was a bad draft pick. That will be true all year." It stayed true for two more years. He was right, I was wrong, and my own verdict is already on the record: "The Anthony Richardson gamble was a bust". What remains is Trevor Lawrence learning a new offense under a coach who at least loves his footwork, Drake Maye in year two with Stefon Diggs, and J.J. McCarthy, who has not yet started an NFL game. That quarterback room has a running tab, and December 2024 collected twice inside eight days: the semifinal, then the third-place game, by 17.70 points combined.

The quarterbacks were not even my worst self-inflicted wound of that season. My son was born in week nine, I left a ruled-out defensive back in my lineup five days later, and Brent, on learning why, announced he would prey on my weakness. Our commissioner, everybody.

Second and not third because six startable wideouts plus Barkley clear tier two on depth alone, whatever the quarterbacks do. The call, since I am only allowed to make them against myself: at least two of my four quarterbacks are not starting NFL games by Thanksgiving. If the ones still standing give me twenty starts of league-average play, this ranking was a coward's ranking. I am at peace with that.

Tier two is the win-now wing: two teams built to take the trophy this year specifically, for opposite reasons, with opposite bills coming due.

Start with the fact nobody says to Brent's face because it sounds like flattery: over the fourteen weeks that set the 2024 standings, the commissioner outscored everybody except Zach. More than me. More than the champion. He went 7-9 anyway, a year after riding nearly the same spine to 12-4, and if you can reconcile those two seasons, the standings have a bridge to sell you. Patrick called for this collapse in writing back in 2023, the oldest roster in the league, a future that "seems inevitable and will be enjoyable for the rest of us", and two years later the collapse is still in the mail. Brent's rebuttal never changes: "It gets younger every year".

It does not, and he knows it does not, and I rank him third anyway because the points keep being real. "There’s barely anyone in my starting lineup that I didn’t trade for" is the most honest self-scout in league history. Lamar Jackson closed August as the MVP favorite. Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the entire Seattle passing game now that the Seahawks handed him the room and a new quarterback. Buffalo just paid James Cook off sixteen rushing touchdowns. Even the punchlines are aging into assets: Nick Chubb, whom Zach declared washed in the middle of the championship game while Brent calmly filed "Chubb is my rb 4", signed in Houston for cheap and walked into the starting job the day Joe Mixon hit the reserve list. The man's fourth running back is now an NFL starter.

And Travis Kelce turns thirty-six on a roster whose owner has bet against time longer than anyone here. Kelce spent the offseason losing twenty-five pounds and getting engaged to the most famous person alive. If the farewell tour has one great season in it, it happens now, in front of every camera on earth.

This roster's resale value is the lowest in the league, and Brent would sign that deal again tomorrow. He gave us the investment thesis himself, in writing: "Live for the now!" The call: Brent outscores his record again, makes the final, and the ring conversation gets very quiet and very serious around Thanksgiving.

The guarantee is the season's premise, so let us price it honestly. It went up on a March night, and Kevin's curse landed before the room went to bed: "You just officially jinxed yourself with the fantasy gods." Between the boast and the curse sits Nate's entire year. And this page's thesis cuts against the favorite too: across the fourteen weeks that decided last season, his scoring ranked fifth while his record tied for second best. Some of that 12-5 was schedule.

The receivers justify the volume. Ja'Marr Chase signed for 161 million in March, briefly the richest non-quarterback deal ever. Malik Nabers shrugged off an August back scare as a minor thing and was full-go for Week 1. Marvin Harrison spent the offseason getting to 220 pounds and admitting out loud that he noticed Nabers and Thomas out-producing him as rookies, which is exactly the sentence you want from a former 1.01 with something to prove. Trey McBride got paid like the best tight end alive in April. Jayden Daniels throws to all of it. Add Hunter, more on him below, and this is the best collection of pass catchers ever assembled here.

Now the backfield, which is a museum of one man's coping mechanisms. Chuba Hubbard is extended and real, and Carolina still went out and signed Rico Dowdle behind him. Brian Robinson, the player Nate literally named his franchise after in the BROBTIME years, got traded to San Francisco in August to stand behind Christian McCaffrey, and Nate greeted it the only way he knows: "Dont forget we are 1 cmc calf strain away from.... BROBTIME." Then, two nights before kickoff, he bought Jerome Ford out of my bench. Ford is a Brown who took a pay cut in May after Cleveland drafted two rookies ahead of him. That is the room: three depth charts' worth of maybes, in a league that starts two backs and a flex.

And the bill from March is still outstanding: the 1.04 that became Hunter cost him his 2026 first and second, and Harlow is holding both. If this season misses, it misses in public, twice.

The call: Nate leads the league in receiving production and finishes exactly where I have him, one rung off the tier he guaranteed. Trophy or crater was always the design. The difference in December is a hamstring.

Tier three runs from here through Karim, and I want to be straight about what it is: six teams the math cannot tell apart. I ordered these six every way I could think of and got a different answer every time. The order below is my judgment, and I expect to be yelled at, which is the point of publishing.

Kevin at five off a 5-12 season is the rank I will defend the hardest. This is the roster the standings have been slandering for years, and the room knows it even while it laughs. Bijan Robinson is coming off 1,887 total yards and Atlanta spent the offseason saying the word explosive. Breece Hall's new coach shut down trade talk in August with an emphatic on-record refusal. A.J. Brown is a three-time All-Pro fresh off a Super Bowl. Tee Higgins got 115 million to stay the best second receiver alive. Tyler Warren, the rookie tight end, spent Colts camp as the safety valve for both quarterbacks. And Caleb Williams gets Ben Johnson, the man who ran Detroit's offense, telling reporters in August that his quarterback was locked in. That is one calendar year of NFL front offices investing in Kevin's starting lineup, one franchise at a time.

There is also this, and I checked it twice because I did not believe it. A week before kickoff, Dallas traded Micah Parsons to Green Bay, where he signed the largest non-quarterback contract in NFL history. We start a linebacker. Parsons is Kevin's linebacker. The room's entire live reaction was two messages. David surfaced to declare "Jerry Jones is my favorite 49ers supporter!", Ben answered "Love that guy", and the chat moved on. Nobody mentioned that the best defensive player of his generation had just become the highest-paid defender alive while sitting on Kevin's roster, where he has been all along. That is the Kevin experience in miniature: the joke goes by, and the quiet man in the corner is holding the punchline. Somewhere in the middle of all this he also started a hot sauce company, announced in April to "Friends and league members (and Nate)", a salutation that is its own scouting report.

The call: Kevin makes the playoffs from fifth, and the man who wrote "Rice for Mclaurin will haunt me the rest of my days" finally gets a December that owes him nothing.

Yes. Sixth. The defending champion, sixth. I will now show my work, because Ben has earned the respect of being argued with instead of crowned.

The championship was real and the final was a classic, 182.28 to 176.58, the closest title game we have ever played, settled by his franchise namesake on a Monday night. "All comes down to my team’s namesake to take me to the promised land. Wouldn’t have it any other way." Then "Finallllllyyyy!", then a superstitious little question about the payout he had been too scared to ask all night, then the updated tally, with Karim's asterisk lovingly preserved. Nobody has ever won this league more quietly or more completely.

But the column's one job is next season, and the numbers under the crown are ordinary. Three teams outscored Ben across the fourteen weeks that decided the 2024 standings. He wrote his own scouting report two years ago, "Im just extremely skilled at getting incredibly lucky", and I remind you he meant it as analysis. The champion's offseason was the same as every Ben offseason, which is to say nearly silent. Joe Burrow opens the year second in MVP odds behind an offensive line Vegas politely calls a problem. Jonathan Taylor now takes handoffs from Daniel Jones. Puka Nacua gets Davante Adams across from him and a bigger role. Garrett Wilson got 130 million from the Jets and Justin Fields at the same time. George Kittle got extended at thirty-one, which matters to a franchise literally named after him. It is a good roster. It was a good roster last year. Good rosters finish sixth when the schedule stops doing favors.

And history is against him in a way this league has felt personally. Karim carried a title into 2023, earned a first-round bye, and still lost twice in December. I carried one into 2024 and did the exact same thing. Nobody has repeated. Standing still after winning is either supreme confidence or a man who knows his luck is a skill and dares not touch anything.

The call, same as it was before I liked him this much: Ben does not repeat. The only man to play in all three finals gets to be furious about this ranking from inside the playoffs, which is exactly how he would want it.

Patrick invented this column's format two years ago, when he ranked all twelve of us twice, once for the present and once for the future, and I am stealing it because he was right: they are different questions. His team is the proof. Present, seventh. Future, top three and maybe better.

The patient man is holding damaged goods this September. Quinshon Judkins went at 1.07 on the draft's second night, and the arrest hit the chat twenty hours later, the slow-draft nightmare the league had voted for arriving right on schedule. As I write this the charge has been declined and the contract still has not been signed. Then Rashee Rice's six-game suspension landed in August, complete with a guilty plea and thirty days of jail attached. Patrick's live reaction remains the driest thing typed all summer: "omg Rashee Rice was suspended no way I had no idea that was possible I am 100% shocked". Those are his two most interesting assets and neither is available in September.

He can afford the wait because he already paid for the lesson. He told us in 2023 about his other dynasty league, all-in for two years, top dog both regular seasons, no title, complete shambles. That kind of tuition buys a man his patience.

Meanwhile the load-bearing pieces are outstanding. Josh Allen is the reigning MVP with a quarter-billion guaranteed, purchased, per the man himself, so he could stop rooting for the Chargers: "Big motivating factor for me was to cut ties with chargers". A man bought the best quarterback in football as a divorce settlement from his own fanbase. De'Von Achane's August calf strain was handled with kid gloves. Bucky Irving's new coordinator is the guy who coached him up as a rookie. The stable runs five deep behind them.

The call: Patrick is above .500 the week Rice comes back. If he is, the six weeks of waiting were the cheapest contention window anyone here has ever bought. If he is not, fifth in the 2024 standings was this team's ceiling and the shambles found him anyway.

I have argued myself into every rank from second to tenth for this team, which has never happened to me before and tells you more about Chudders than the eight does.

The haul is real. Eleven picks, headlined by Ashton Jeanty at the 1.01, who went sixth overall to the Raiders and was handed a backfield. Emeka Egbuka at 1.05, whom Baker Mayfield spent camp calling an absolute stud while injuries cleared Tampa Bay's receiver room for him. Colston Loveland at 2.01, the tenth pick in the NFL draft, walking into a Ben Johnson offense that lives in two-tight-end sets. Jahmyr Gibbs was already here, and Detroit's new coordinator says the plan is Gibbs and Montgomery on the field together. Justin Herbert gets a second straight year in the same offense. That is a genuinely frightening core, and outside the quarterback none of it is older than twenty-three.

The case for eight instead of five is that rookies miss, and Matt knows it better than anyone, because the league watched Jeanty's preseason debut go for minus one yard on three carries and reacted the way we react to everything Chudders. The case for eight instead of eleven is that this rebuild has already survived its darkest timeline. Two last-place scoring seasons in three years bought this draft class. His July self-portrait as the Kevin Costner of this draft was a bit that keeps getting truer.

One receipt to carry into the season: Nate has been short Jacory Croskey-Merritt since August, telling Matt to be "sell sell selling JCM aka BiLL", and Washington's first September depth chart listed Bill fourth even after they traded Brian Robinson away to clear the room. Somebody is going to be very right by October.

Two calls, because this team finally deserves the respect of real ones. Chudders is not last. And Chudders wins more games than in any season in franchise history, which sounds grand until you remember the record to beat is six.

Oscar's roster is a garage sale of other franchises' decisions, and I mean that with admiration. Seattle sold DK Metcalf to Pittsburgh for a second-round pick; he immediately signed for 150 million and gets Aaron Rodgers at forty-one. San Francisco sold Deebo Samuel to Washington for a fifth. Kansas City's suspension problem just made Xavier Worthy the deep threat of the defending AFC champions for six weeks, a development Oscar prepared for years ago with the finest scouting note ever filed here: "Extremely valuable scouting note you won’t get anywhere else: Xavier worthy is fast". Buying what other teams quit on is a real strategy with one failure mode, which is that sometimes they quit because the player is cooked, and you cannot tell from the receipt. Tank Dell's knee is the grim version of that sentence.

But the spine of this team, for the first time, is stuff Oscar drafted himself. Omarion Hampton went 1.02 here and 22nd overall to the Chargers, where the veteran ahead of him opened camp on the injury list because of a fireworks accident, of all the ways to inherit a job. TreVeyon Henderson arrived at 1.06 while Oscar was in a work fire drill, courtesy of the clock, and the accidental prize aged well fast: New England's coordinator spent camp flexing Henderson out wide to hunt matchups. Brock Bowers caught 112 balls as a rookie, the most by any rookie ever at any position. That is a first-team All-Pro and two first-round backs, none of it secondhand.

The quarterback room is C.J. Stroud, Justin Fields and Michael Penix, and Oscar has already picked his faith: "It’s finally his year.  Penix about to pop off" is the official religion of a 3-13 franchise, and Atlanta at least agrees enough to have Penix locked in as the starter.

The call: Oscar finishes ahead of at least two teams ranked above him on this page, and he will be the first to remind me which two.

Karim owns the two loudest single data points in league history and the widest gap between best case and likely case on this page.

Data point one: the 2022 banner, which is real no matter how many asterisks Ben glues to it. Data point two: week eleven of last season, when he hung 248.26 on Kevin, the highest score any of us has ever posted. It was so undeniable that both keepers of the league's records stood down on the spot. Zach: "Congrats Karim. No asterisk there. Just an all time week". Ben, of all people: "Even I will admit there's no asterisk on that monster week 🫡". Karim's acceptance speech, naturally: "From hence forth I am forever the weekly champion". Ben's contribution was to muse that his own team would have found a way to put up 249 had he been the opponent that week, and Zach priced the miracle exactly: "Probably 248.27". One hundredth more than required. The entire Ben religion in a decimal.

He also collected the offseason's only cease-and-desist. He drafted Cam Skattebo the day after Nate traded away the chance, floated "Shall I change my team name to #SKATTABOTIME?!?!", and then pushed his luck with #THORTONTIME until Nate's lawyers, per Nate, got involved. The suffix is Nate's registered trademark from the BROBTIME years, which is exactly why Karim keeps borrowing it.

The roster that produced that night still photographs like a contender. Amon-Ra St. Brown, pried out of Oscar in the November trade that reset both franchises. Mahomes, whose offense spends October without Rashee Rice and openly plans to go deep more. Waddle, due a bounce-back with Tyreek's wrist rebuilt. And Christian McCaffrey, fully cleared in July after playing four games last year, managed all camp on scripted rest days by a coaching staff that says out loud it must protect him from himself. San Francisco was worried enough about the room behind him to trade for Brian Robinson in August.

That last sentence is the whole ranking. When McCaffrey plays, this team's ceiling is the record book, see above. The floor is 2024, when the ceiling appeared for exactly one November evening and the rest was a 7-9 shrug. Tenth is what a medical file is worth. "Champs don’t calculate" is the counterargument and honestly it has won before.

The call: fifteen McCaffrey games makes this ranking look three spots too low, and Karim gets to say so all winter, from the UK, with interest.

Tier four is two franchises whose best season is not this one, and they know it.

The joke wrote itself in 2023: the team was named Father Time because it was genuinely old, second oldest in the league by Patrick's audit, and its signature move was overpaying for Brock Purdy, which Karim graded as "a Purdy pile of trash". Two years later the man they mocked for buying Purdy watched San Francisco hand the same quarterback 265 million dollars in May. David is a 49ers fan. He has never once said I told you so, which somehow makes it worse for everyone. The man types like he is signing documents. "Ooo I guess I Win; sorry Karim" is his idea of trash talk, semicolon included.

Now look at the roster. Brian Thomas Jr. put up 87 catches and 1,282 yards as a rookie. Ladd McConkey broke Keenan Allen's Chargers rookie records. Rome Odunze spent August as Caleb Williams's two-minute-drill security blanket. Tetairoa McMillan went eighth overall to Carolina as exactly the big target Bryce Young was missing. The oldest-named franchise in the league quietly assembled the youngest great receiver collection any of us has ever held, and Zach called the strategy in real time: "Burgers got the blueprint quietly over there. Stacking young wideouts for 2-3 years". Brent's version was blunter: "Burger is wide receiver island".

The island has no bridge. Three running backs, total, in a league that starts two plus a flex. Nate is running the same wideout-rich, backfield-poor experiment seven spots up this page, and the gap between them is instructive: Nate's receivers are finished products with a proven quarterback attached, and Nate answers the phone. The best of David's three backs, Jaylen Warren, at least enters the year as Pittsburgh's lead back for the first time. Five quarterbacks for one slot, including two rookies from the same class, one of whom, Jaxson Dart, torched the preseason and got named QB2 in New York while Shedeur Sanders sat fourth string behind a forty-year-old. The surplus is the most obviously tradeable thing in the league, owned by the one man who does not answer the phone. Patrick has tried. Nate has tried. The island does not take calls.

The call: David does not trade a single quarterback before the deadline, and it costs him a playoff spot. The fortune still lands in 2027, right on schedule, and he will greet it with a semicolon.

Twelfth, by a hair, and it is the first ranking on this page I would trade back.

Start with what Harlow actually is, because the team name, a three-way pun on his rookie haul of Luther Burden, Trevor Etienne and Woody Marks, undersells him: the most rigorous evaluator in this league. He sets numeric bars. He once accepted a trade he did not even want just to see if the other man would honor his own offer. When a rule the league had voted in earlier that season was used to force his hand in a lost December, he pointed out, correctly, that he was the one soaking in everyone else's mess, "I’m just sitting downstream drinking in the sewer water of your tanking ramifications", then said "But I’m an honorable person and will do it", and complied. The man's process is cleaner than his luck.

And the luck has been biblical. He was the March seller who handed Nate the 1.04 for a package fronted by Rhamondre Stevenson, and his stated price tells you he was playing a longer game: "Mondre was a throw in, next years 1st was the cornerstone for me". Kevin scored the bout in real time, "Congrats Harlow, you’ve won the trade", and here is the thing: if the guarantee craters, Kevin is right forever. Harlow holds Nate's 2026 first and second. He is the only man in this league with a genuine short position on the season's loudest bet, and shorts pay best in a crash.

The 2025 lineup is why he is down here anyway. Justin Jefferson, the best player on the roster, spent camp nursing a hamstring and gets a first-time starter at quarterback. Brandon Aiyuk opens on the reserve list until at least October. George Pickens is the upside swing, freshly moved to Dallas across from CeeDee Lamb in a contract year. The backs are James Conner, entering his age-thirty season off genuinely elite tackle-breaking numbers, and Isiah Pacheco in a four-man Kansas City room. The quarterbacks are Kyler Murray, who gave Arizona six games of genuinely high-level play last year and won five of them, against eleven lesser ones that produced eight losses, and Tua. It is a roster of real names one year early or one year late, which has been Harlow's whole story here.

The call, against my own order: Harlow finishes ahead of David, and I spend the winter explaining why I ranked the short position last.

paragraphs: This league has always written its own power rankings. Karim graded us all by type of garbage. Ben gave every team a Reason for Hope and a Reason for Despair. Zach addressed his like a will. Patrick ranked every roster twice, now and five years out. Oscar handed out power levels from sacko to lich king. I buried all twelve of us in Thanksgiving metaphors in 2023, a piece of writing I would pay real money to un-publish. The tradition survived me. Now it lives here.

So, season four. Three seasons, three champions, none of them twice. Ben finally broke through last December in the closest final we have ever played, 182.28 to 176.58 over Zach, and became the third man to try defending a title, after Karim could not and I could not. The offseason that followed produced 182 transactions, an eleven-day rookie draft, one arrest, one motion against the commissioner that never found a second, and one cease-and-desist letter over a hashtag. Dues are $250 now, collected on the honor system, and Matt has already told us where the money goes: "I accepted long ago that all our dues were used to purchase SOL".

Here is what I finally understood this summer, after three years of squinting at our standings: they are lying to us. Brent went 7-9 last season while outscoring everybody but Zach across the fourteen weeks that decided the year. Kevin went 5-12 with a starting lineup the NFL spent the whole offseason extending and building around. Ben went 13-3 while three of us outscored him. Our records are the points plus a coin flip, and I am done ranking the coin.

So this year the rankings come in four tiers, because pretending I can order the middle of this league is exactly the kind of confidence the last three seasons have punished. Where the future disagrees with the present, I will say so out loud, an idea I stole from Patrick's 2023 edition, the way everything good here eventually gets stolen. The scoreboard for the order itself is the only one that matters: who is most likely to win this season.

And over all of it hangs one sentence, typed into the chat on a March night by a man who had just paid his 2026 first, his 2026 second and a starting running back for the right to chase it: "do yall understand im about to win a Jailyard fantasy football championship in 2025?" Kevin cursed it the same night. The rest of us get eighteen weeks to find out whether the fantasy gods take the case.
Positions below. Several will look stupid by Halloween. That is the job.
sections.title: Season Four

paragraphs: The league voted for its first slow draft, twelve hours a pick, and I treated the clock as a feature. My reasoning eventually went on the record: "It's supposed to be a slow draft and every minute you can delay a pick is advantageous. Never know when the next story like Judkins will hit the wire". By the time I typed that, the strategy already had its body count, and the body was Patrick's.

The wire went off on the third night, hours after Patrick's 1.07 was already locked. Oscar posted it first: Quinshon Judkins, arrested, unsigned, Cleveland. Patrick had drafted him roughly twenty hours earlier and signed off with "Now I can go to bed". Zach said the quiet part for everyone: "Ooooff. That’s the risk of starting the draft so early". Karim reposted the same story at his London breakfast, hours stale, and Brent filed it under "Typical British behavior". Nate, campaigning as ever against the men who burn the full clock, turned the arrest into an argument: "Browns didn't have the luxury of waiting until week 1 of the nfl season to decide on judkins. Same in dynasty." Patrick's epilogue came in August when prosecutors declined the case: "Thank god my top pick is not a criminal, probably just a huge piece of shit of a guy." The contract, as I write this, remains unsigned.

Matt owned the 1.01 and had been on the clock in spirit all offseason. "I'm literally Kevin Costner in Draft Day right now", he announced, fielding calls, while Harlow coached the room from the cheap seats: "Lowball his ass". Matt took Jeanty. Oscar took Omarion Hampton at 1.02 on purpose, a distinction that matters because at 1.06 he was in a work fire drill and the clock took TreVeyon Henderson for him. His scouting report on his own auto-pick is the most honest sentence in draft history: "Wasn’t the guy I would have taken but probably going to be my best player now". David, surveying all of this from the island, asked the only question that needed asking: "Are we getting another auto draft?"

I would like to skip the next part but the record is the record. At 1.09 I fat-fingered Kaleb Johnson, demanded an undo, studied the board while the league enjoyed itself, and issued the greatest walk-back in draft history: "Actually looking at everyone, I’m good". The misclick made the pick. Analytics.

Then came the Ferguson Violation. Kevin's consolation-bracket prize, a compensatory 2.13, had no slot on the Sleeper board, so he called his pick out loud, "Rams tight end t ferguson", and the room agreed to work around it. Matt set the protocol: "okay so we all just dont pick ferguson". Zach saw the future: "This is gonna get dicey when someone accidentally autodrafts Ferguson". He was wrong only about the accidentally. David, the quietest man in the league, read the board, understood precisely what was sitting on it, and took Terrance Ferguson on purpose. Kevin's scouting desk: "Sprinted that pick to the podium". Karim went straight to sentencing: "Fine him!" Brent reversed the pick by hand, with no rule to cite, because there is no rule. It remains the only ruling in league history that moved a player from one roster to another. Nate's response arrived the following evening: a formal motion to challenge Brent for the commissionership in 2026, which needed two seconds to reach a vote and collected zero, plus one "Nay" from Kevin an hour after the point was moot.

Eleven days, seventy-two picks, one arrest, zero friendships forfeited. Matt's wife met Patrick Surtain at a conference mid-draft and Matt had her scout his own pick in person, which is the most Chudders sentence ever written and also, technically, the league's first field report.
sections.title: Eleven Days in July

paragraphs: The best argument this league produced all year happened on a Friday afternoon in July, and one piece of history explains the heat: nobody in this league has ever traded a kicker, a defense, or an IDP player. Not once. Those slots have no market because the waiver wire restocks them for free every Sunday morning, which is correct pricing. Then Jacksonville drafted a first-round talent Sleeper tags as both WR and DB, the one player those slots have ever produced that another owner might genuinely covet, and the room had to invent a price in real time.

Kevin found the door in February, five months before anyone walked through it: "Sleeper will count Travis hunter’s offensive stats when he’s in the DB slot. Official" He even filed the definitive scouting line: "He’ll be Jalen Ramsey but with the talent Jalen Ramsey thought Jalen Ramsey had". Then July came, Nate spent the 1.04 on the loophole Kevin had posted, and Kevin spent the rest of the summer arguing against acting on his own discovery, which deserves some kind of award.

The afternoon itself produced actual analysis. Brent asked the right question: "If he doesn’t play much at db then what’s his value as a db on ur roster". Zach answered with a number: "You have a DB who gets 10 points a game on offense". Harlow confirmed the baseline, "10 points is pretty standard for a DB", and Brent, who concedes more gracefully than his reputation allows, gave it an "Ah that’s fair". Ten points. Three men agreed, out loud, on what an ordinary starting DB hands you for free.

Then Harlow set the bar at "He needs to average 15+ to be better than good DB IDP’s", half again the number he had just called standard, and nobody flagged the gap. Nobody except Kevin, who did the arithmetic instead of the vibes: "He needs to average 4-60-0.4tds to be worth it as a DB play". Run that line through our scoring and it lands at 10.4, almost exactly the baseline Zach and Harlow had named. The sharpest skeptic in the league asked the pick to clear a bar it never needed to clear, and the man who got the number right spent the whole afternoon on the other side of the trade. Kevin's real objection is the one that survives: "He doesn’t tackle either. So no points from that. Only INTs". Tackles are the one thing a cornerback produces every single week. Nate sold a floor to buy a ceiling, which, to be fair, is the same trade he makes everywhere.

The first evidence is already in, in miniature. In Hunter's preseason debut, Jacksonville played him ten snaps at receiver with the starters and eight at corner with the backups. The experiment is live, on television, weekly.

And then the conversation stopped being about football, which is when it got interesting. Ben, the sitting champion, put the endgame in writing: "we can also always just collude against Nate and get rid of the db spot if it becomes too much of a cheat code". Nate's reply was the most honest thing he said all summer: "However I didn't calculate yall turning on me and getting rid of db slots!" If that sounds far-fetched, consider that the actual NFL spent this spring trying to do the identical thing to Philadelphia. The Packers proposed banning the tush push, a legal play that one team is simply better at than everyone else, and in May the owners fell two votes short of outlawing it. Legislating away another man's edge is a grand old football tradition. Nate is one bad December and eleven votes from finding out how it feels.

For the record, the argument was also conducted with expert witnesses. Nate consulted the most agreeable authority available: "ChatGPT doesn't lie. I told it I can use thunters offensive stats in my db slot...." Ben, concurring in part: "ChatGPT lies all the time lol". Kevin, footnote for the ages: "It’s also very sycophantic". The season will not resolve which of them is right about the machines. It will absolutely resolve who was right about the corner.
sections.title: What a Defensive Back Is Worth

paragraphs: Every running joke in this league eventually routes back to November 2023, and most of us now tell it in shorthand. Here it is in full one time, because season four cannot be understood without it.

Nate was 3-5 with his season slipping. He drew David that week. He benched his starters. Zach called it live: "Solid intentional tank by Nate against burger this week. May have just earned himself the number 2 pick". Patrick, who does not raise his voice, raised it: "Oh, snap, when people said Nate was tanking today, I didn’t think he was actually doing it", followed by the institutionalist's objection, "Obvious reason #2 why tanking sucks. It inequitably impacts playoff and playoff seeding races". Kevin filed the coldest line in league history: "Last season we tanked with class". Oscar made it permanent in his power rankings with "a curse upon BRO". And Ben wrote the whole constitutional crisis: "No one's saying you broke any rules. We just hate what you're doing and are going to make new rules to prevent it."

Nate's defense is still on the record and he has never withdrawn a word: "Team chudders started Jaylin Hyatt. Father time started zeke eliot. All backups. I can keep going. I'm not tanking. Im starting the same caliber of players most managers are starting weekly. I feel you should be able to decide your own starting roster week to week."

The forgotten hinge of the whole affair is Brent. The emergency vote came down to the commissioner, the loudest anti-tanking voice in the room, and he voted no, against his own side, on principle, then threatened the defendant in the same breath: "I’m voting no, but @Sacko stop tanking now, play your best line up or I’ll let them to vote to boot you. I don’t want to have this conversation again." The rules that eventually did pass were built by the aggrieved: Kevin hand-built the max-points rule that now sets our draft order, and then watched it grind him personally through an unlucky 2024. There is a lesson in there about writing laws while angry.

The epilogue arrived thirteen months later and almost nobody clocked it. On the night Ben won the title, Nate cheerfully told the room about his other league: "I started a dynasty league with my ohio friends, and purposely didnt draft any rbs besides for a few rookies. It was an all natural 1st year tank job to get Jeanty. Could win that league for the next 5+ years in a row." The man who swore for a year that he never tanked here described his tank there the way a chef describes a signature dish. Karim spoke for the room: "Lolz the master tanker".

Two years on, the defendant is ranked fourth in this column, owns the best receiving corps we have ever seen, and has tried, so far without finding a single second, to put the commissionership of the man who spared him up for a vote. Nothing was forgiven, nothing was ruled on, and the place would be unrecognizable without him.
sections.title: The Tank

paragraphs: The last message of our offseason was mine, on September 3, and I stand by it: "Is Trevor Lawrence really going to be able to support two WR1s? As a TLaw owner, I’m very skeptical". I own Trevor Lawrence. Nate owns Travis Hunter, one of the two receivers in question. So the final word of the offseason was one man publicly shorting another man's investment while appearing to fret about his own.

So here is the table as the lights come up. Zach has the points and my blessing, which he must now survive. Brent has never had a better roster or less time. Nate has a guarantee, four receivers, and a prayer at running back. Kevin has the league's quietest great roster and a linebacker who just became the highest-paid defender alive. Ben has the crown and three years of history saying nobody keeps it. Patrick is waiting out a suspension on purpose. Matt finally has a team. Oscar has other people's discards and his own two first-rounders. Karim has one medical file between himself and the record book. David has 2027 on layaway. Harlow is short the guarantee and long the receipts.
The games start Thursday. Good luck this season, everyone. You all look terrifying.
sections.title: Thursday
